lessons.title: BASIC Comes Home
intro: In 1975, two young programmers, Bill Gates and Paul Allen, wrote a BASIC for the Altair 8800, one of the first home computers. It was the first product of their company, Microsoft.

Soon almost every home computer came with BASIC built in: the Apple II, the ZX Spectrum and the Commodore 64 from 1982, the best-selling home computer ever. When you switched one on, it greeted you with READY. and you could start programming right away.

These BASICs looked very much like what you've learned. LET became optional, a colon allowed several statements in one line, and new commands added graphics and sound. Programs like the one below run on both.

code: 10 REM RUNS AT DARTMOUTH AND ON A C64

exercises.prompt: Which company started with a BASIC for the Altair 8800?
exercises.explanation: Altair BASIC from 1975 was Microsoft's very first product.

exercises.prompt: What did a Commodore 64 show right after switching it on?
options: Nothing until a disk was inserted
exercises.explanation: The computer started straight into BASIC, just like the screen of this app.

exercises.prompt: On a C64, this line works. What's different from Dartmouth BASIC?
options: The line number is too small
A is not a valid name
exercises.explanation: Home computer BASICs made LET optional. At Dartmouth in 1964, it was required.

exercises.prompt: What does the colon do in this C64 line?
options: It puts two statements in one line
exercises.explanation: The colon separates statements, so PRINT and GOTO share line 10. This line prints HI forever.

exercises.prompt: Why did BASIC become so popular in the 1980s?
options: It came built into almost every home computer
It was the only language that existed
exercises.explanation: Millions of kids typed their first programs into a home computer's BASIC, often copied from magazines.

exercises.prompt: Which of these did home computer BASICs add that the 1964 original didn't have?
exercises.explanation: PRINT, FOR and line numbers were there from the start. Graphics and sound came with the home computers.

lessons.title: The Same Ideas in Python
intro: Python is one of the most popular languages today, and almost everything you learned carries over. The words are different, the ideas are the same.
PRINT "HI" becomes print("HI"). LET X = 5 becomes x = 5. FOR I = 1 TO 10 becomes for i in range(1, 11): and IF X > 5 THEN becomes if x > 5:
There are no line numbers. Instead, the lines that belong to a loop or an IF are indented. GOTO doesn't exist at all, and GOSUB with RETURN becomes a function made with def.

exercises.prompt: This is the example program in Python. What does it print?
exercises.explanation: It's the same program as the BASIC example: the numbers 1 to 10 add up to 55.

exercises.prompt: Why does Python write range(1, 11) for the numbers 1 to 10?
options: The end value of range is not included
exercises.explanation: range(1, 11) stops before 11. FOR I = 1 TO 10 in BASIC includes the 10.
Python's print works like BASIC's PRINT, written in lowercase with parentheses.

exercises.prompt: What tells Python which lines belong inside a loop?
options: The indentation at the start of the line
exercises.explanation: Indented lines belong to the loop or IF above them. There's no NEXT, the indentation ends the loop.

exercises.prompt: Which Python feature is closest to GOSUB and RETURN?
exercises.explanation: def creates a named block of code you can call from anywhere, and it can even return a value, like DEF FN.

exercises.prompt: Which BASIC line does this Python code match?
options: IF S >= 50 THEN, followed by a PRINT "PASSED" line
exercises.explanation: Same decision, same comparison. Python can just put the action right under the if instead of jumping to a line.

lessons.title: What's Next
intro: You've learned the language that brought programming to millions: output, variables, decisions, loops, lists, subroutines, functions, input, text, and how to find bugs.
Those ideas are the foundation of every programming language. In Python, JavaScript, Java or Swift, you'll recognize all of them, just in new clothes.
The best next step is to build things: small games, calculators, tools for your own life. You know how to break a problem into steps. That's the real skill.

exercises.prompt: Which of your BASIC skills will you need in other languages?
options: All of them: variables, decisions, loops, lists, functions and debugging
None, modern languages are completely different
exercises.explanation: The words change, the ideas don't. That's why a first language is never wasted.

exercises.prompt: This loop is JavaScript. Which BASIC line does it match?
exercises.explanation: Start at 1, keep going while i is at most 10, and add 1 each round. Exactly FOR I = 1 TO 10.

exercises.prompt: In Python, scores = [72, 45, 90] creates a list. What's the BASIC way?
options: DIM S(3) and READ the values from a DATA line
There are no lists in BASIC
exercises.explanation: Python writes the list directly. In BASIC, you'd fill S(1) to S(3), for example with READ in a loop.

exercises.prompt: Who created BASIC at Dartmouth College in 1964?
exercises.explanation: Kemeny and Kurtz wanted every student to be able to use a computer, not just scientists.

exercises.prompt: What's the best way to keep getting better at programming?
options: Build small projects you actually care about
Wait until you know everything before starting
exercises.explanation: Every project teaches you something new, and finished projects are the best motivation.

options: Basic Automatic System for Internal Calculation
exercises.explanation: The B for Beginners says it all: BASIC was made so anyone could learn to program. Now you have.
